hero.title: File:USS West Alsek (ID-3119).jpg
hero.credit: U.S. Naval Historical Center Photo #: NH 102368
hero.description:
SS West Alsek (American Freighter, 1918)
Underway during builder's trials, off Seattle, Washington, on 4 June 1918, while painted in pattern camouflage.
Built in 78 working days by the Skinner & Eddy Corporation, of Seattle, this steamship was acquired by the Navy on the day of her trials and placed in commission as USS West Alsek (ID # 3119). She was returned to the U.S. Shipping Board on 27 January 1919.
The original print is in National Archives' Record Group 19-LCM.

U.S. Naval Historical Center Photograph.

gallery.title: File:USS West Apaum (ID-3221).jpg
gallery.credit: "NH 102369 SS West Apaum". U.S. Naval Historical Center.
gallery.description:
SS West Apaum (American Freighter, 1918)
Underway during builder's trials, off Seattle, Washington, on 19 June 1918. She was constructed in 78 working days by the Skinner & Eddy Corporation, of Seattle.
This steamship was acquired by the Navy on 20 June 1918 and placed in commission as USS West Apaum (ID # 3221). She was returned to the U.S. Shipping Board on 25 July 1919.
Note her "dazzle" type pattern camouflage.
The original print is in National Archives' Record Group 19-LCM.

U.S. Naval Historical Center Photograph.
categories: Black and white photographs of ships

gallery.title: File:SS West Arrow.jpg
gallery.credit: U.S. Naval Historical Center Photo #: NH 83443-A
gallery.description: 5,589 GRT cargo steamship West Arrow under way. Skinner & Eddy Corp of Seattle, Washington built launched her as J.C. Eddy on 23 May 1918. She was considered for acquisition by the US Navy in World War I and assigned the registry ID # 2585, but was not taken over.The US Shipping Board renamed her West Arrow and owned her until 1935, when the British shipping company Cairns, Young and Noble of Newcastle-upon-Tyne bought her and renamed her Black Osprey. The German submarined U-96 sank her in the North Atlantic in 1941.The original print is in National Archives' Record Group 19-LCM.US Naval Historical Center Photograph.
categories: Black and white photographs of ships

gallery.title: File:SS West Lianga.jpg
gallery.credit: U.S. Naval Historical Center Photo #: NH 65075-A
gallery.description:
West Lianga (American Freighter, 1918)
Underway off Seattle, Washington, on 4 May 1918, the day of her trial trip and delivery. Built by the Skinner & Eddy Corporation, Seattle, she had been constructed in 67 working days (79 calendar days).
This ship was acquired by the Navy on 19 August 1918 and placed in commission the next day as USS West Lianga (ID # 2758). She was returned to the U.S. Shipping Board on 24 June 1919.
The original print is in National Archives' Record Group 19-LCM.

U.S. Naval Historical Center Photograph.

gallery.title: File:West Ekonk underway.jpg
gallery.credit: U.S. Naval Historical Center Photo #: NH 65041-A
gallery.description:
West Ekonk (American Freighter, 1918)
Underway, probably during her trials in July 1918, while painted in pattern camouflage. She had been launched by the Skinner & Eddy Corporation shipyard, Seattle, Washington, on 22 June 1918, after being on the building ways for only 57 work days.
Delivered by her builder on 13 July 1918, she was placed in commission the same day as USS West Ekonk (ID # 3313). The ship was returned to the U.S. Shipping Board on 9 April 1919.
She later became British merchant ship SS Empire Wildebeeste and was sunk during World War II.
The original print is in National Archives' Record Group 19-LCM.

U.S. Naval Historical Center Photograph.

gallery.title: File:Skinner & Eddy shipyard, ca 1917 (MOHAI 6353).jpg
gallery.description:
In 1916, the Skinner & Eddy Corporation opened a shipyard at the foot of Massachusetts Street on the site of the old Moran Brothers yard. Skinner & Eddy built 75 vessels during World War I, becoming Seattle's largest shipyard. The end of the war, in 1918, brought a depression in shipbuilding, and the yard was sold in 1923.
This photo of the Seattle waterfront shows the Skinner & Eddy shipyard. The coastal steamer "Orizaba" and a battleship are in port for repairs. In the distance are the Centennial Mill Company's flour mill (left) and the beginnings of Harbor Island (right). Judging by the size of the filled-in Harbor Island, the photo was probably taken between 1916 and 1918.
Written on back of photo: "Former site of Skinner-Eddy's Ship-Yards later taken over by U-S-A for repair yards."
Subjects (LCTGM): Boat & ship industry; Piers & wharves; Ships

gallery.filename: The Town Crier, v.13, no.51, Dec. 21, 1918 - DPLA - d6b2b4987f3aae4e654ef7259bdb34d7 (page 3).jpg
gallery.title: File:The Town Crier, v.13, no.51, Dec. 21, 1918 - DPLA - d6b2b4987f3aae4e654ef7259bdb34d7 (page 3).jpg
gallery.description: Annual Christmas number. Cover illustration by Irene Ewing. Page 3 includes photograph of the Times Square Building at 5th Ave. and Olive Way. Page 23 includes photo of the launching of the S.S. West Madaket from the Skinner & Eddy shipyard. Pages 24-25 include more ship photos and an article on the topic of shipbuilding. Page 30-37 article ""Highways and Byways of Our Town"" describes features of Seattle and includes photographs from Wayne Albee, Webster and Stevens, M. Chase and Daniel Huntington and artwork by Edward Forkner and D.J. Myers. Page 44 article ""Seattle's Legacy"" and Page 59 article ""Seattle's Industries in 1918 and 1919"" discuss Seattle war industries and opportunities for expansion. Page 47 article ""A David Out of the West"" profiles Skinner and Eddy general manager David J. Rodgers. Page 48 article describes the rapid growth of Rainier Valley. Page 57 article ""Holiday Impressions of Long Ago"" describes historic Seattle holiday celebrations. Page 71 article "Big Orders for Vulcan" discusses the Vulcan Manufacturing Company.
